sec.title: Purpose
sec.p: The purpose of this study was to investigate the contribution and natural progression of ABCA4 deep intronic variants (DIVs) among a Chinese Stargardt disease (STGD) cohort.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: For unsolved STGD probands, DIVs in ABCA4 were detected by next-generation sequencing, and splicing effects were evaluated by in silico tools and validated through minigene experiments. Comprehensive ocular examinations, especially fundus changes, were carried out and analyzed. These and long-term follow-up data were compared with data of patients carrying biallelic coding variants of ABCA4.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Seven DIVs in ABCA4 were identified in 18 of 40 (45.0%) unsolved STGD probands, involving 2 novel and 5 known variants. Four DIVs were confirmed to effect splicing through minigene assay. The c.161-395G>A was the most prevalent DIV allele (30.6%, 11/36). In the early 5-year duration, localized maculopathy was predominant, accounting for 51.9% (14/27) of fundus recordings. Expanded macular lesion within the vascular arch, with or without flecks, was observed in 75.0% (12/16) of recordings beyond the 5-year duration, whereas generalized retinal dystrophy was rarely observed. Compared with those in the non-DIV group, the patients in the DIV group manifested milder fundus change at all disease stages (P < 0.05). Follow-up visits utilizing wide-field fundus autofluorescence (FAF) further validated the slower development of lesions. Optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) documented a gradual reduction in perfusion in each layer's capillaries and high-reflective deposits below the sub-RPE layer.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: DIVs contribute to nearly half of STGD cases with missing heritability, totally occupying 7.8% of all STGD families. Based on optimized grading criteria, patients with DIV alleles manifested localized macular lesions with slow progress. The amount of residual correctly spliced mRNA might play a role, suggesting that adding or enhancing normal ABCA4 expression might be a potential approach of intervention.

body.p: Stargardt disease (STGD), as one of the most frequent inherited retinal disorders, poses a profound threat to central vision among juveniles. Autosomal recessive STGD is the most predominant form and is attributed to biallelic variants in ABCA4 (STGD1, OMIM #248200).1 Variants located in the coding regions and flanking splicing sites of ABCA4 account for 60% to 70% of STGD families, whereas the remaining cases have been typically detected as having single or no pathogenic variants in ABCA4.2,3 Deep intronic variants (DIVs) in ABCA4 have been found to explain missing heritability in these unsolved families, with approximately 10% of STGD cases that could be ascribed to DIVs.4,5 However, it is difficult to detect and assess DIVs by the current commonly utilized genetic testing, that is, exome sequencing (ES). DIVs in ABCA4 have been confirmed to result in the inclusion of pseudo-exons, through strengthening cryptic splice sites, creating novel splice sites or strengthening splice enhancer elements in introns, simultaneously leading to low-abundant transcript messenger RNA (mRNA) and/or protein defects.4,6 Such aberrant splicing effects of DIVs differ from those of canonical splicing site change variants, and varying degrees of wild-type mRNA transcripts remain.7 Moreover, the ratio of correctly to incorrectly spliced transcripts caused by different intronic variants has been noted to influence the clinical manifestations of patients with DIVs.8 The phenotypic heterogeneity of ABCA4 has been revealed to represent a sequential progression of a single disease reflected by the varied fundus manifestations.9 Based on these findings, it is interesting to uncover the genetic origins and clinical features of unsolved STGD families within our Chinese STGD cohort. Furthermore, exploring the correlation between the level of splicing of DIVs and phenotype severity through follow-up studies was essential for effective diagnosis and intervention.

This study enrolled 40 STGD families for whom no definite genetic causes were identified by routine ES. Among them, DIVs in ABCA4 were detected in 18 families (45.0%) by genome sequencing (GS) or enhanced ES. Patients carrying DIVs exhibited milder fundus manifestations at all disease stages (P < 0.05) than patients with STGD carrying biallelic ABCA4 variants in the coding region. Long-term follow-up of 13 patients with DIVs revealed the slower progression of macular lesions. It was proposed that the severity of the phenotype was determined by the varying degrees of residual correctly spliced mRNA due to DIVs. The milder phenotype revealed in patients with DIVs prompts us to address the essential role of the amount of correctly spliced mRNA in the ultimately prognosis and intervention efficiency of STGD, which is critical for the development of upcoming therapeutic strategies targeting ABCA4-related conditions.

sec.title: Participant Enrollment and Data Collection
sec.p: Approved by the Institutional Review Board of Zhongshan Ophthalmic Center, our study enrolled individuals diagnosed with STGD or identified with biallelic pathogenic variants in ABCA4 from the Pediatric and Genetic Clinic, Zhongshan Ophthalmic Center, Guangzhou, China. Available family members were also included. Clinical data, detailed ophthalmic examinations, and peripheral venous blood samples were collected from the participants and family members after they signed the informed consent forms in accordance with the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki. The method used to extract genomic DNA from leukocytes in peripheral venous blood was consistent with a previously described procedure.10

sec.title: Deep Intronic Variant Detection and Evaluation
sec.p: The genomic DNA of all probands was subjected to targeted exome sequencing (TES) or whole exome sequencing (WES).11 Of 252 unrelated STGD families, biallelic variants in the coding region of ABCA4 were identified by routine ES in 212 families, as published in our previous study.9 These families composed the non-DIV group in the present study. The remaining 40 probands, who exhibited clinical features of STGD, but in whom a definite cause was not identified, were collected for further analysis, including 37 probands that initially underwent WES and 3 probands that underwent TES. Of these, 24 probands were selected for GS,12 including 17 probands in whom a single pathogenic variant in the coding region of ABCA4 had been identified and 7 in whom no pathogenic variants had been identified. Building upon the results of the GS, a total of 42 probes targeting DIVs were added to our ES panel (NEXome Plus Panel version 1.0; Nanodigmobio, China; Supplementary Table S1). Sixteen of the 40 STGD probands were subjected to ES with the extended panel that included additional probes to detect previously unidentified DIVs.

The potential splicing effect of DIVs in ABCA4 was assessed by SpliceAI (https://spliceailookup.broadinstitute.org/) and the RNA splicer prediction tool on the Rare Disease Data Center (RDDC; https://rddc.tsinghua-gd.org). Both are deep-learning tools assessing the splicing defect of non-coding variants by predicting whether the splice junctions from random pre-mRNA transcript sequence was changed.13,14 Input chromosome positions and nucleotide changes, the SpliceAI software generates a splice Delta score ranging from 0 to 1, which is interpreted as the probability of the variant having an effect on splicing. Variants with a Delta score greater than 0.2 were considered to be appropriate for in vitro experimental confirmation. As for the second prediction tool, RDDC, the gene and the coding DNA reference sequence for the variant were queried. The RNA Splicer tool on the RDDC website displays alternative splicing results. Predicted Delta scores higher than the raw values with significant differences indicate that the inserted sequence is present in the form of a pseudo-exon. Furthermore, DIVs were evaluated through a comparative analysis among the 3 groups: (1) the STGD cohort comprising 252 probands diagnosed with STGD from our clinic (including 212 families in the non-DIV group published in our previous study9 and 40 unsolved families enrolled in this study); (2) the in-house control group consisting of probands with variable ocular conditions; and (3) the general population from the gnomAD database (version 4).15 All variants were subsequently confirmed by Sanger sequencing16 as well as co-segregation analysis among available family members (Supplementary Table S2). For families in which co-segregation analysis could not be completed, the gnomAD co-occurrence tool (https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/variant-cooccurrence) was utilized to evaluate the probability of a trans configuration.

sec.title: Minigene Assay of Novel DIVs
sec.p: The DIVs were performed with minigene assays to validate splicing abnormalities.17 Their putative splicing effect was functionally analyzed with the pcDNA3.1-based exon trapping system.18,19 Each wildtype and mutant minigene construct was designed by amplifying the genomic region encompassing the intron carrying the variant and flanking exons using a 2×T8 High-Fidelity Master Mix polymerase. Oligonucleotide primer pairs flanked by BamHI/EcoRI and NotI restriction sites were utilized. Then, the amplified products were cloned into the pcDNA3.1 vector. HEK293 cells were transfected with 2 µg of construct DNA using Lipofectamine 3000 DNA transfection reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and harvested after 24 hours, and the total RNA was extracted using the Trizol-based method. The extracted RNA was subjected to reverse-transcription (RT)-PCR using the PrimeScript RT reagent Kit with gDNA Eraser (Takara, Japan). The acquired cDNA, both mutant and wildtype, was analyzed by RT-PCR. The RT-PCR conditions were as follows: an initial denaturation at 95°C for 5 minutes, followed by 35 cycles consisting of 30 seconds at 95°C for denaturation, 30 seconds at 62°C for annealing, and 30 seconds at 72°C for extension. A final extension step was performed at 72°C for 10 minutes. A pair of primers targeting a segment sequence located in the promotor region of the pcDNA3.1 plasmid were designed as a transfection control and Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GADPH) was selected as a housekeeping gene control. Primers located in the upstream and downstream flanking exons of DIVs were used (Supplementary Table S3). In the cell transfection and RT-PCR process, one well of the six-well plate was used as a negative control. No plasmid was introduced into this well, and it was processed alongside the other wells containing DIV plasmids throughout the culture and RT-PCR procedure. After separation by electrophoresis on 2% agarose gel and purification using the TIANgel Midi Purification Kit (TIANGEN, Beijing, China), the sequence of each band was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The grayscale for correctly and incorrectly spliced bands of each DIV captured by electrophoresis was semi-quantified utilizing ImageJ software.

sec.title: Clinical Data Review and Characterization
sec.p: Clinical data, particularly those of the DIV group, were analyzed in detail, including age of onset (AO), best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA, Decimal), routine fundus photography, posterior fundus autofluorescence (FAF) examination, autofluorescence images captured by ultra-wide scanning laser ophthalmoscopy, optical coherence tomography (OCT), optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA), and full-field electroretinogram (ERG). The area of the macular lesions of all probands was quantitatively calculated by ImageJ (https://imagej.net/ij/).

sec.title: Literature Review and Statistical Analysis
sec.p: All reported DIVs of ABCA4 in the literature were collected through a search using the keywords “ABCA4” and “deep intronic variants” on PubMed (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/, accessed on August 1, 2024) and reviewing the Human Gene Mutation Database (HGMD; https://www.hgmd.cf.ac.uk/ac/validate.php) and the Leiden Open Variation Database (LOVD; https://databases.lovd.nl/shared/genes/ABCA4). The clinical recordings, focusing primarily on the AO and BCVA, of each reported patient with STGD carrying DIV in ABCA4 were reviewed. Statistical analysis and visualization were performed with SPSS Statistics (version 25.0). The comparison of the fundus grades between the DIV group and the non-DIV group were analyzed by Fisher's exact test, and the Mann-Whitney U test was used to compare the AO of the non-DIV and DIV groups. Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05.

sec.title: Contribution of DIVs in ABCA4
sec.p: Forty unrelated STGD probands, in each of whom a single variant or no pathogenic variants were detected in the coding region of ABCA4 through routine ES (37 with WES and 3 with TES), were collected, comprising 25 families in whom a single variant was identified and 15 in whom no pathogenic variants were identified. Of the 40 families, 24 were sequenced with GS, and 16 underwent enhanced ES with additional DIV probes. A total of 18 (45.0%) families was successfully resolved with GS or enhanced ES technology. All 25 families detected with a single ABCA4 variant in the coding region were sequenced by GS (18) or enhanced ES (7). Of these, a single DIV was detected in 17 families (68.0%), including 11 families solved by GS and 6 by enhanced ES. The other 15 STGD families, in whom no pathogenic variants were detected, were sequenced using enhanced ES. Of these, only one proband was identified with a homozygous DIV in ABCA4. No families were detected with a single DIV. In total, families carrying DIVs accounted for 7.8% (18/230) of our 230 solved STGD families (included 212 families described in our previous publication9; Fig. 1).

This table exhibits the minor allele frequency (MAF) in the gnomAD database, allele count (AC) in our STGD cohort, prediction results using the two in silico tools (Splice gain scores of SpliceAI greater than 0.2 and significantly higher predicted values of alternate splicing in RDDC indicate a potential impact on splicing for the DIVs), RNA, and protein changes of the seven DIVs identified in our cohort. Although co-segregation analysis was not available for 3 pedigrees, one is homozygous and the trans configuration for the remaining 2 families was estimated based on the gnomAD co-occurrence information of ABCA4, revealing that the 2 heterozygous pLoF variants identified in Family 27006 was unlikely to be in a cis configuration. Family 28606, which was identified with a pLoF in combination with a weak missense variant pair, had an extremely low probability of being in cis, estimated at approximately 1 in 10,000.

sec.title: Minigene Assay Result of DIVs
sec.p: Seven pathogenic DIVs in ABCA4 were identified, including five previously reported (c.161-395G>A, c.2919-826T>A, c.4539+1100A>G, c.4634+741A>G, and c.5461-1321A>G) and two novel DIVs (c.1937+188A>G, and c.3329-551C>G). Variant c.161-395G>A had one allele recorded in the gnomAD database (version 4), but the other 6 DIVs were absent from the general population database. All 7 DIVs had Delta scores of more than 0.2 in SpliceAI and obtained a predicted value significantly higher than the raw values in the RDDC tool, indicating a splicing effect with a pseudo-exon inclusion (see Fig. 1). Individuals from the 18 solved STGD families were verified by Sanger sequencing. The trans configuration was further confirmed through available co-segregation analysis in 15 of the 18 families (Supplementary Fig. S2). Of the remaining three families, one showed a homozygous variant and the configuration of the remaining two families lacking co-segregation data was estimated based on the gnomAD co-occurrence tool, which indicated an extremely low likelihood of these variants occurring in cis. Additionally, the possibility of a complete intron deletion in the homozygous family has been excluded (Supplementary Fig. S3).

Five previously reported DIVs have been demonstrated to affect splicing through minigene experiments.6,7,20–23 In our study, minigene experiments on four DIVs, including two novel (c.1937+188A>G and c.3329-551C>G) and two reported (c.161-395G>A and c.4634+741A>G), revealed pseudo-exon inclusions or partial intronic retention of varying sizes. RT-PCR experiments for the four DIVs were repeated in triplicate. In the mutant construct of two DIVs (c.3329-551C>G and c.4634+741A>G), two bands were observed: one corresponding to the correctly spliced mRNA transcript and the other to the aberrantly spliced transcript. Three bands were observed in the mutant fragment for the c.161-395G>A and c.1937+188A>G variants. Three incorrectly spliced mRNA transcripts, with pseudo-exon inclusions of different sizes (PE1b, PE1c, and PE1d), were confirmed in the mutant construction of the c.161-395G>A variant. For the c.1937+188A>G variant, an exon elongation of 187 nucleotides (IR2) as well as a pseudo-exon inclusion (PE2) could be identified. Semi-quantitative analysis of the RT-PCR results revealed that the incorrectly spliced bands for the 4 DIVs accounted for more than 50% of the total intensity (the sum of the grayscales of the correctly and incorrectly spliced bands; Fig. 2, Supplementary Fig. S1). The most frequent DIV among our patients with STGD was c.161-395G>A, located in intron 2, with an allele frequency of 30.6% (11/36) in the probands identified with DIVs, accounting for 11/19 (57.9%) of all DIV alleles. This result differs from the literature, which has predominantly focused on Caucasian patients. Summarized from 65 published studies listed in Supplementary Table S4, a total of 736 families have been identified with DIVs in ABCA4. Of the DIV alleles, the most prevalent was c.4253+43G>A with an allele frequency of 19.1% (152/797) and the majority of reported DIVs were clustered in introns 30 and 36, accounting for 26.1% (208/797) and 17.1% (136/797), respectively (see Fig. 1, Supplementary Table S4).6,24,25

caption.p: Minigene assay results of four deep intronic variants (DIVs) in ABCA4 identified in our cohort. (A) Schematic representation of the 4 DIV fragments cloned into the pcDNA3.1(+) vector. Each of the four DIVs was modeled with wildtype (WT) and mutant (MUT) minigenes. Exons are depicted as pink rectangular boxes. The positions of the DIVs are indicated with asterisks. The WT and MUT products of each DIV minigene are displayed on the right. The WT construct exhibits normal splicing of exons without residual intronic inclusions, whereas the mutant forms of the four DIVs show a pseudo-exon (PE) insertion or intron retention (IR), represented by fractions of blue intron boxes between the exons. (B–E) Wildtype and mutant minigene assay results were analyzed using agarose gel electrophoresis and Sanger sequencing. RT-PCR for the WT fragment demonstrates a normal splicing. RT-PCR for the mutant bands show splicing defects with different sizes of pseudo-exon inclusions or partial intron retention (C). In the presentation of the sequencing results, the exonic regions were highlighted with pink and the retained intronic regions were marked in blue, in order to better demonstrate the breakpoints connecting the exons with the retained intronic regions. The amount of both correctly and incorrectly spliced mRNA for each DIV was roughly quantified based on the results of agarose gel electrophoresis and is presented below the gel. The Sanger sequencing results of both the correctly (a) and incorrectly (b, c, and d) spliced fragments for each DIV are displayed on the right of the agarose gel electrophoresis images.

sec.title: Clinical Characterization of DIVs in ABCA4
sec.p: In total, 22 patients from the 18 families were identified with DIVs in ABCA4. The gender ratio of males to females was nearly equal, with 12 male patients and 10 female patients. Their median AO was 11.0 years old (interquartile range [IQR] = approximately 8.0 to 18.0), which is older than that of the non-DIV group (median = 9.0, IQR = approximately 6.0 to 12.75, P = 0.05) but younger than that of the patients carrying DIVs in the literature (median = 18.0, IQR = approximately 10.0 to 42.0, P = 0.008; Supplementary Fig. S4A).26–28 Follow-up visits were available for 13 patients, including 12 patients with long-term follow-up over 3 years, with the longest period being about 10 years, whereas one proband had a follow-up of 1 year (Supplementary Table S5). A total of 42 BCVA recordings were enrolled, of which 24 recordings were obtained within a 5-year duration, ranging from 0.1 to 0.7 (median = 0.20, IQR = approximately 0.15 to 0.30). The median BCVA in cases of longer disease duration (6–12 years) was 0.10 (IQR = approximately 0.07 to 0.15), ranging from 0.04 to 0.3. No significant statistical differences in the age of examination and BCVA were observed between the DIV and non-DIV groups (P = 0.87 for age and P = 0.38 for BCVA). Comparison with the 104 available BCVA data of patients carrying DIVs collected from the literature revealed that our patients carrying DIVs exhibited an earlier age of examination (median = 12.0, IQR = approximately 11.0 to 16.8) than these published patients (median = 38.5, IQR = approximately 21.3 to 53.0, P = 1.08E-10), whereas no statistical differences in BCVA were observed (see Supplementary Fig. S4B).

Based on the grading criteria of STGD proposed in our previous study,9 this study utilized papilla disc (PD) units to quantitatively measure the macular lesions. The grading system was optimized as follows: stage I shows a macular hypo-autofluorescence lesion localized in the foveal and parafoveal region (approximately 1 to 2 PD units in diameter); stage II exhibits a lesion limited within the macular vascular arch (3 to 5 PD units), with or without flecks in hyper- or hypo-autofluorescence change; stage III is characterized by an extended atrophied area beyond the vascular arch (6 to 10 PD units); and in stage IV, the lesion is larger than 10 PD units in diameter with pigment deposits. All 22 patients with DIVs underwent fundus examinations during their initial visits. Moreover, 13 patients had additional fundus photography during follow-up visits, including 6 patients who had at least 3 follow-up visits and 7 patients who were examined twice, resulting in the collection of a total of 43 fundus recordings captured during different disease durations (see Supplementary Table S5). Compared with the patients in the non-DIV group (also including images collected during follow-up visits), significant statistical differences were identified (P < 0.05) at visits during each duration period. Of 27 fundus recordings from patients in the DIV group taken within the 5-year disease course, 14 recordings were classified as stage I (14/27, 51.9%) and 13 as stage II (13/27, 48.1%). For images from patients in the non-DIV group, also within a 5-year duration, the majority (61.8%, 84/136) were classified as stage II (P = 0.03). Twelve fundus recordings from the DIV group were obtained during the 6- to 12-year disease period, of which 9 (75.0%) were categorized as stage II. Whereas stage IV was common, as the same with stage II, in patients from the non-DIV group within the same disease course, accounting for 40.9% (18/44; P = 0.008). Of the fundus recordings obtained at a duration of more than 13 years, 2 of the 3 from the DIV group were classified as stage II, whereas one was classified as stage IV. In contrast, 87.5% patients (21/24) from the non-DIV group with more than 13 years duration exhibited changes consistent with stage IV (P = 0.009). In view of the diameter of the macular dystrophy area, a relatively slower progression as the disease advanced in patients from the DIV group was observed through the fitted curve (Fig. 3, see Supplementary Fig. S5) and further confirmed by long-term follow-up visits.

sec.p: Wide-field FAF imaging revealed that patients from the non-DIV group had more extensive lesions than patients from the DIV group during the same course in both the early and late stages (Fig. 4, Supplementary Fig. S6). More widespread hypo-autofluorescence flecks that scattered throughout the entire retina were observed in five patients with a disease duration of over the years, suggesting a significant progression of the disease (Fig. 4, A6–A8, Supplementary Fig. S6, A2, A3). The OCT results of 20 patients from the DIV group revealed varying degrees of thinning of the entire retina in the macular area, accompanied by high-reflective deposits, without obvious differences from comparison with those in the non-DIV group (Supplementary Fig. S7). Twelve patients underwent OCTA at their last visit. As the disease progressed, an increase in the non-perfusion of the small capillaries at the margins of the superficial and deep vascular complex, along with a larger foveal avascular zone, was observed. In the outer retinal choriocapillaris (ORCC), sub-RPE, and choroidal vascular plexus, a reduced density of capillaries and an increased accumulation of the hyper-reflective materials deposits in the fovea area were observed (Fig. 5). ERG examinations were conducted on five patients, of whom four exhibited moderately reduced cone responses and normal to mildly reduced rod responses, whereas one had normal cone and rod responses. The clinical data for patients carrying DIVs, which are not included in the main figures, have been presented in Supplementary Table S6.

caption.p: Posterior fundus auto-fluorescence from patients of the DIV group at follow-up visits and comparison of the wide-field auto-fluorescence manifestations between patients in the DIV and non-DIV groups. Long-term follow-up visits and wide-field FAF of each patient from the DIV group are denoted with the letter A and located within the blue dotted box. Wide-field fundus imaging from patients in the non-DIV group is labeled with B and located within the red dotted box. The disease duration (expressed in years) is displayed at the bottom right in each figure. Slower development and more localized macular dystrophy lesions were observed in all patients from the DIV group in different disease duration stages. More widespread hypo-autofluorescence flecks were present in patients A6 to A8 with a duration of at least 10 years than that in patients A1 to A5 with disease courses of less than 10 years.

Optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) of patients from the DIV group in our cohort. As the disease progresses, the perfusion of the small capillaries at the margins of the superficial and deep vascular complex decreases. Additionally, the density of capillaries in the outer retinal choriocapillaris (ORCC), sub-retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and choroidal vascular plexus are reduced, accompanied with deposition of highly reflective materials. With disease progression, the choroidal vessels are significantly exposed due to the atrophied retinal layer, accompanied by deposition of highly reflective materials. The right arrowhead indicates the disease duration (expressed in years). The OCTA examination results of normal control (NC) were presented in the first line, serving as a reference for the patients.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study delves into the missing heritability in STGD, with a focus on the DIVs of ABCA4, which account for nearly half of the unsolved STGD cases and 7.8% of all ABCA4-associated STGD families, highlighting their considerable role in STGD. The phenotypic characteristics of patients with STGD identified with DIVs of ABCA4 were comprehensively clarified through detailed ophthalmic examinations, long-term follow-up visits, and comparison with patients carrying biallelic coding variants of ABCA4. A later AO and more limited macular dystrophic lesions with slower progression were observed among patients with DIVs. Specific advanced manifestations on OCTA of STGD were demonstrated for the first time. Additionally, our understanding of the association between the level of splicing effects and the phenotypic severity among these patients with DIVs has been enhanced.

Because it was proved that DIVs alter the transcripts of ABCA4, it has been increasingly recognized that DIVs in ABCA4 play a role in the missing genetic causality among patients with STGD.4,7 The contribution of DIVs in our STGD cohort aligns with the solved rates of DIVs observed in Caucasian STGD cohorts, accounting for 7.9% to 17.9%.3,4,6,27,29,30 The c.161-395G>A variant was considered to be a region-specific founder variant within the Chinese population, whereas in Caucasian patients, the DIVs located in intron 30 were most prevalent.6,8,27,31 Two novel DIVs were verified to induce a defect in splicing by minigene assay, broadening the spectrum of DIVs in ABCA4 and emphasizing their functional significance in the context of aberrant splicing. Variants in two STGD-phenotype related genes, BEST1 and PRPH2, have been thoroughly evaluated in our previous studies,32,33 and this study aims to complete the genetic spectrum of STGD. To achieve this, variants in three additional genes associated with a STGD-like phenotype were examined, including ELOVL4, TIMP3, and RIMS1. No pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) variant in these genes were identified in our STGD cohort (Supplementary Fig. S8). To evaluate unsolved STGD families, examination of difficult to detect variants in ABCA4, including copy number variations, deep intronic variants, noncanonical splicing site changes, and frequent hypomorphic variants, is still an important avenue to identify the underlying molecular causes.24

Extensive research has sought to elucidate the genotype-phenotype correlation of ABCA4 variants. These studies have mainly focused on variants in the coding regions and provided valuable insights into disease severity and prognosis.5,34–36 The clinical manifestations largely depend on the residual activity of ABCA4, determined by the combination of alleles, where variants in ABCA4 have been categorized into null, severe, moderate, and mild.36–38 Some frequent DIVs were also included in the perfect genotype-phenotype correlation matrix of ABCA4 established on the disease prognosis, of which c.4253+43G>A was categorized as rare hypomorphic with mild prognosis, c.4539+2001G>A was classified into the moderate class, and c.5196+1056A>G variant was considered to be severe.35 The level of incomplete splicing effects of DIVs, more commonly referred to as the ratio of correctly to incorrectly spliced mRNA transcripts, has been proposed to directly influence clinical outcome.8 In the current study, the second alleles in 17 out of the 18 families were coding variants classified as P/LP based on ACMG/AMP criteria, including 5 truncation variants and 12 missense variants with high prediction scores. Compared with patients carrying biallelic P/LP variants in the coding region of ABCA4, those carrying DIVs, leading to incomplete splicing effects and varying levels of abnormal mRNA transcripts, exhibited milder STGD phenotypes featuring slowly progressive and sharply demarcated RPE atrophic lesions relative to non-DIV patients with the same disease duration. Although the limitation of the HEK293T artificial model in simulating the real genetic environment or cellular background of the retina persist, the correlation between the mild manifestation observed among patients carrying DIVs and the incomplete splicing effects as estimated by the functional experiments was consistent with the findings from previous studies using the patient‐derived induced pluripotent stem cells.39,40 Certainly, utilizing a more realistic retina-specific model to investigate the quantitative relationship between splicing effects and phenotypic severity among a large STGD cohort can be expected in future studies. Notably, more widespread hypo-autofluorescence flecks were observed in patients with longer disease durations who carried different DIVs. This was also noted in patients carrying biallelic coding variants,9 suggesting that it is important to consider disease duration when evaluating the severity of variants.

A total of 13 patients were identified with the same DIV (c.161-395G>A), including 12 in compound heterozygous status and one in homozygous status. This group provides an ideal opportunity to conduct a comprehensive genotype-phenotype correlation analysis to reveal variant-specific phenotypic severity. Eleven of the 12 patients in compound heterozygous status displayed consistently milder fundus change regardless of the second allele, which aligns with findings from a recently published case of a patient with the same c.161-395G>A variant.23 Only one proband (27006-II1) carrying c.161-395G>A in trans with a canonical splice-site change variant (c.6479+1G>C) presented severe fundus change (stage IV) over a period of more than 10 years. The consistently milder phenotype of c.161-395G>A might be explained by the “clinical dominant” phenomenon, where hypomorphic alleles with greater remaining function determine a milder phenotypic outcome.35 Previous studies have also observed a significantly milder phenotype in a subset of patients with one identical DIV in trans with varying null variants.8,40 Proband 28780-II1 is the first patient identified with the extremely rare c.161-395G>A variant in a homozygous status to date, which provides valuable insights into the phenotype characterization for this particular variant. This patient experienced minimal visual impairment until 18 years of age, with a preserved visual acuity of no worse than 0.3 and localized macular atrophy, showing no progression over 4-year follow-up visits, which was similar to the phenotype described as mild previously.41 Minigene experiments of the c.161-395G>A variant revealed an abnormal transcript level exceeding 50%, suggesting that over 50% of all transcripts were affected in homozygotes, which was considered sufficient to result in the mild phenotype. Although the quantitative relationship between the threshold of the deep intronic variant's effects on splicing and their impact on the phenotype remains uncertain for now, it is imperative to investigate the certain threshold of functional protein reduction determined by the combination of variants in future. Additional impacts by factors such as the genetic background, environmental effects, and cis-acting modifiers, could also influence the phenotype.2,42–44 With multiple studies underway to investigate potential treatment avenues for STGD,5,45 antisense oligonucleotide-based splicing modulation exhibits excellent potential in the treatment of patients with STGD carrying DIVs.6,31 Our findings suggested that patients carrying DIVs exhibiting milder phenotypes may be outstanding candidates for interventions to achieve a more favorable therapeutic outcome.

In summary, DIVs in ABCA4 contributed to nearly half of the unsolved STGD cases and accounted for about 7.8% of all the families. The contribution rate of DIVs observed in our Chinese cohort aligns with the rates identified in previous studies among Caucasians, highlighting the crucial role of DIVs in ABCA4 as an important underlying cause of STGD and calling for more attention to DIVs in future research and clinical practice. Furthermore, the clinical features of patients with STGD carrying DIVs were thoroughly explained from variable perspectives. The valuable finding that the DIV group showed a relatively localized macular lesion with slower progression provides insight into interventions. The amount of correctly spliced mRNA of DIVs in ABCA4 proved to be a determinant factor of the milder phenotype, which suggests that supplying the normal expressed ABCA4 protein or repairing the incorrectly spliced mRNA offers a therapeutic direction.
